young.html: After the Trojan War, the Greek heroes sailed home. One of them, clever Odysseus, king of the small rocky island of Ithaca, took ten more years to get there. The Odyssey is the story of that trip, and of his wife Penelope and son Telemachus, who waited for him.

On the way, Odysseus meets wonders and monsters: a one-eyed giant called a Cyclops, a witch named Circe who turns his men into pigs, singing Sirens whose song lures sailors onto the rocks, and a six-headed monster and a whirlpool on either side of a narrow strait. He gets out of trouble mostly by thinking. He tells the Cyclops his name is "Nobody", so that when the giant shouts for help, he cries, "Nobody is hurting me!" and no one comes.

young.cap: Follow Odysseus' voyage stop by stop. Most of the places are legends; the map shows where ancient and modern readers have guessed they were.

young.html: At home, a crowd of rude young men are eating up his food and pestering Penelope to marry one of them. She tricks them for years: she says she will choose after she finishes weaving a burial cloth for Odysseus' father, and every night she secretly unpicks what she wove that day. When Odysseus finally comes home in disguise as an old beggar, the first to know him is his old dog, Argos.

Draw your own odyssey. Draw a map of a trip you have taken, even to the park or a grandparent's house. Mark the stops, and give each one an adventure (real or made up). Then tell the story to someone, starting in the middle, the way Homer does, and go back to explain how you got there.

full.html: The Odyssey, like the Iliad, comes from the oral poetry of early Greece and is credited to Homer; it probably took its present shape a little after the Iliad, around 725 BC. It has 24 books and about 12,100 lines of hexameter verse. Where the Iliad is about a few weeks of war, the Odyssey is about getting home, and about who a person is when no one recognizes him.

full.text: Tell me, O muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy.
full.author: Homer

full.html: Odysseus' usual epithet is polytropos, "of many turns", which Butler renders as "ingenious". He is the hero of cunning, disguise and patience. It was his idea, in later tellings, to build the wooden horse that ended the war.

The poem does not start at the beginning. Books 1–4 follow Telemachus, now grown, as he travels to find news of his father. Book 5 finds Odysseus himself, kept for seven years on the island of the nymph Calypso. Freed at last, he is shipwrecked on the island of the Phaeacians, and in Books 9–12 he tells his hosts the story of his wanderings. Books 13–24 bring him home to Ithaca.

full.cap: The wanderings of Books 9–12, then home. Step through the stops and read what happened at each.

full.html: At the Cyclops' cave, Odysseus is trapped with his men by the giant Polyphemus, a son of the sea god Poseidon. When the giant asks his name:

full.text: Cyclops, you ask my name and I will tell it you; give me, therefore, the present you promised me; my name is Noman; this is what my father and mother and my friends have always called me.
full.author: Homer

full.html: The trick saves them, but as he sails away Odysseus cannot resist shouting his real name. Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon, and the god's anger is the reason Odysseus' journey takes so long. Cleverness wins; pride costs.

Athena, the goddess who loves Odysseus for his intelligence, disguises him as an old beggar. He tests who has stayed loyal: the swineherd Eumaeus, his son, his old nurse Eurycleia (who knows him by a scar), and his dog.

full.text: As soon as he saw Ulysses standing there, he dropped his ears and wagged his tail, but he could not get close up to his master. … but Argos died as soon as he had recognized his master.
full.author: Homer
full.note: Butler uses the Latin names: Ulysses for Odysseus, Jove for Zeus, Minerva for Athena. Shortened where marked.

full.html: Penelope sets a contest: whoever can string Odysseus' great bow and shoot through twelve axe heads may marry her. Only the beggar can. Odysseus then fights the suitors, with Telemachus beside him, and wins back his house. Penelope still tests him herself: she asks for their bed to be moved, and he angrily says it cannot be, because he built it around the trunk of a living olive tree. Only the two of them knew that.

Guest-friendship (xenia). The Greeks held that strangers and guests must be welcomed, fed and helped, and that Zeus protects them. Much of the Odyssey tests this rule: the Phaeacians and Eumaeus keep it; the Cyclops and the suitors break it.
Thinking Odysseus spends all twenty years at sea. Ten years were the war at Troy. Of the ten years coming home, seven were spent on Calypso's island.

deep.html: Ithaca is a real island in the Ionian Sea, but Homer's descriptions of it don't fit it perfectly, and people have argued since ancient times about the geography of the poem. Ancient writers already placed the Cyclops in Sicily and Scylla and Charybdis at the Strait of Messina. The geographer Eratosthenes (3rd century BC) joked that you would find the scene of Odysseus' wanderings when you found the cobbler who stitched the bag of winds. The map in this lesson shows traditional guesses, not facts.

Some scenes are grim: the Cyclops eats several of Odysseus' men, and the end of the poem includes a harsh punishment of the suitors and of servants who sided with them. Readers have long debated whether Odysseus' revenge goes too far. The poem itself ends with Athena stopping a new cycle of fighting and making peace.

items: Is Odysseus a hero, a trickster, or both? Is lying ever the right thing to do?
Penelope is as clever as her husband. Who is the real hero of the poem?
What makes a place home? Why does Odysseus turn down Calypso's offer to make him immortal?
What do we owe strangers who come to our door?

deep.html: Later writers kept sailing with Odysseus. Virgil's Aeneas visits some of the same places. In Dante's Inferno, later on this ladder, Ulysses tells of a last voyage beyond the known world. Tennyson's poem "Ulysses" (1842) has the old king ready to set out again.

questions: Odysseus gets out of the Cyclops' cave by a trick, then nearly ruins it by boasting. When has showing off cost you something?
Penelope waits twenty years and keeps her suitors guessing. What qualities does she need for that?
The dog Argos knows Odysseus when no one else does. Why do you think Homer put that scene in?
Which adventure would you most like to have had, and which would you most like to have avoided?
How should guests behave, and how should hosts? Which characters in the Odyssey get it right?
care: There are some frightening and violent scenes (the Cyclops, and the fight with the suitors at the end, including a harsh punishment of disloyal servants). The voyages of Books 9–12 and the homecoming scenes with Telemachus, Argos and Penelope suit young readers best.
